p:
Great. Thank you.

JACK FOGLE:It just, you know– it's never been stress-tested by DOT, but DOT continues to insist, and you'll hear the rest of the testimony to that. It's— somebody's going to die. And I'm, you know, unless somebody's chasing ambulances in the street, literally, physically.
We appreciate your testimony. Thank you. Ma'am? Just turn on the mic.

Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Lynette Lauretig, and I am the co-founder of the River Arts Viaduct Project Rescue Committee. I co-founded this committee due to an experience that I had outside the River Arts building, which I will be brief and explain. I was in the lobby of my building when a group of EMS workers came in looking very frustrated, confounded, and upset. They had been trying to get into our building for at least 15 minutes, could not find or access the entrance because of a call that somebody had made for a partner of someone who was having a heart attack. Once they got into the building, they found their way quickly to the apartment. But again, I'm talking about the same situation that Jack technically explained, but I'm giving you my experience

personally about this. I had just retired from working for the city for 25 years and was looking forward to spending time with my grandchildren until I realized that the work had stopped at our building and there was no contractor, nothing was happening, no progress, and so I decided to start this committee. I'd like to talk about the numbers of residents we're talking about here amongst the three buildings. In River Arts, we have 500 residents, 60 percent are over the age of 60. So you can imagine how many times EMS gets called. River Terrace right next to us has 2,500 residents and the James has 500. We're looking at this project affecting 3,500 residents alone. The impact to these residents are serious and extensive, from delays in EMS, as we have said, to residents who actually have limited mobility and have to climb three flights of stairs to exit the building. Honestly, I believe that we have been lucky so far, very lucky. It's been seven years, but we're running out of luck, and people need to recognize that, or this is going to blow up. Trust me. Thank you very much.
Thank you for your testimony.

Thank you for the opportunity to testify here today. Thank you to all the Council Members and especially to Majority Leader Abreu, for generating this opportunity. As you heard from Jack and Lynette, one of the complications here of this stalled project is a life and safety issue. Plain and simple, it's a life and safety issue. What I'm afraid of is that the DOT or Judd Law will try and fix the life and safety issue and ignore the larger— the larger project, the issue completing the job. We have— you know, my lens is through the Community Board 12 from my position there as a member. For the last year— I've only been on the community board for a year— but for the last year, I have been listening to the representative of the DOT show up at the traffic and transportation meetings. And to every answer is– speaking of things, Chair Restler, that piss you off— this pisses me off. Here are his answers to our pointed questions. Well, that's an ongoing conversation. I'll have that answer for you next month. I'll let you know. I'll share this with my colleagues. And especially, thank you for letting me know. And that was in response to a very simple question about the existence of– the status of the

job as it was. There's no reason in the world that he wouldn't have known that. Oh my God. I have a statement from Dr. Eliza Miller, who is a vascular neurologist, a stroke doctor, who— it'll be submitted to the record. But there's— just very quickly. We put together from the Community Board an eight-page document saying just open up this section in front of River Arts It'll obviate the need to jerry-rig the emergency access. It's completed in front of River Arts. There's 490 feet that are completed. All they have to do is stripe it and open it up. It's in the hands of the DOT. It's been there through Councilman Abreu's office since the middle of March. And we have not heard a peep from them since then. It's a simple answer to a complicated question, and I look forward to hearing from them. Thank you so much. And that document will be submitted to you as well.

I really– I just want to thank you all for taking— each of you for taking the time to speak with us today, share your expertise, highlight this issue. I think with your advocacy and the Majority Leader's advocacy, we clearly got it on the radar today of the senior people at DDC and DOT, and with a new administration

that's much more ethical and competent and responsive, I think we're hopeful that we'll see real results and improvement because this is clearly an issue that needs immediate attention. So thank you all. We really appreciate it.
The statement by our vascular surgeon is really important. It needs to be— I don't know if you have time for it, but–
We appreciate it very much. We'll take a look. So thank you.
Thank you guys for coming. I'll see you around.

We will move to some cultural institutions. David Lowey from Brooklyn Academy of Music. Hopefully you'll get completed in time for the gala tonight. Steven Lazickas from Carnegie Hall, Michael Schnall from the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, all CIGs, and we'll also bring up Lucy Sexton from New Yorkers for Culture and Arts. You know what, why don't we add a fifth chair, if that's okay? And we'll include Jeremy Kaplan from Encore Community Services as well. Feel free to testify in whatever order y'all are so moved.

Sorry, do you mind? I think my computer's going to die if I don't testify first. I am Lucy Sexton, New Yorkers for Culture and Arts. I want to thank the Chair, the Majority Leader, the Deputy Speaker for this critically important hearing and for including the culture sector in this discussion. Cultural centers are central to our communities and our city. We serve as economic engines, community anchors, and infrastructure for our civic life. The cultural community actually included capital funding reform as part of our sector-wide budget ask. Now, why is a capital reform a budget ask? Because, as you've heard, the current system takes enormous resources from cultural organizations, with project delays requiring us to take out loan after loan and wind up costing so much more than originally budgeted. So yes, this is a budget ask, and one that, if implemented, would also save the city money. The ask is threefold. One, create transparency, update the Open Data portal for capital projects at cultural institutions which has not been updated since 2021. B, plan responsibly. Develop a capital infrastructure plan for culture. Better planning would allow all organizations to

build and maintain infrastructure more efficiently. Identify key process improvements that would allow cultural organizations to leverage city capital funding in timely and efficient ways. I want to add by saying this is also an equity issue. Smaller organizations in low-wealth communities are less able to access large private funding, therefore more dependent on city support, and have less capacity to take on the debt, the bureaucracy involved in the city's capital process. Every community has the imagination required to make art and create culture, but to quote Sade Lythcott of National Black Theatre, who spoke on a panel last week, imagination without infrastructure disappears. So to the slogan on my t-shirt, "Culture for All," I want to add my new slogan, "Infrastructure for All." Thank you.

Good afternoon. My name is Mike Shnall. I'm the Director of Government and Community Affairs at Brooklyn Botanic Garden. I'm just going to cut to the chase. BBG experiences— our experience with the city capital process is all too familiar to many of our cultural fellow cultural institutions. BBG accounts for escalation in addition to what the city recommends is an eight percent

compounded percentage each year, along with other expenses that come with the capital process that can make a project considerably more expensive than what we originally budgeted. A few examples of the systemic issues we've experienced: capital reimbursement processes can create cash flow challenges for nonprofits. Profits that must front costs while awaiting city reimbursement. Difficulty with auditors who don't understand construction contract terms can hold up reimbursements indefinitely. Two, coordination between city agents can be inconsistent, creating duplicative review processes and unclear accountability. For example, a DDC project manager sometimes asks for modifications to standardized forms, which can put the process on hold. And lastly, small and midsize organizations, like Lucy said, often lack the administrative capacity to navigate the highly technical and lengthy capital process, limiting equitable access to city capital funds. BBG often has to work with outside cost consultants to help with the heavy lift of grant administration, which the organization would otherwise be unable to handle internally. In summary, the CIGs are just asking– as the stewards of some of

New York's most treasured public assets, these capital processes often make it extraordinarily difficult to maintain these facilities. And all we're really asking for is not less oversight, but in fact clearer timelines, better coordination between the institutions and the city, allowing public projects to move at a pace our communities and our constituencies deserve. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker, Majority Leader, and Chair. My name is Steven Lazickas, and I have the pleasure of serving as the manager of government relations at Carnegie Hall. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. Carnegie Hall shares our colleagues' gratitude for the city's continued investment in capital improvements for cultural organizations. These invaluable funds support projects that protect historic assets, improve accessibility and affordability, and ensure our institutions can continue serving New Yorkers for years to come. These projects help safeguard our buildings, our audiences and the tens of thousands of cultural workers in New York City. Carnegie Hall shares our colleagues' vision for a more unified,

efficient, and timely capital contracting process, and join in their ask for the City to improve and reform the capital process in the following ways: increasing transparency by updating the Open Data portal, planning responsibly by developing a capital infrastructure plan for culture, and identifying key process improvements to make it more efficient and less burdensome for our institutions. The current process is slow, unpredictable, and burdensome. Due to contract registration and reimbursement spanning several years, Carnegie Hall has been forced to front costs for expensive projects, and as the Deputy Speaker mentioned, we carry nearly $200 million— or $200 million— geez, $2 million per year in interest alone while we wait through the CCG process on our current facade restoration project. For example, also our DDC elevator modernization project took nearly six years from appropriation to contract registration, and we could not receive final payment until August 2025, more than seven years after the funds were appropriated. Along the way, documentation requirements have escalated and shifted without clear and consistent guidance, such as subcontractor approval packages that grew from 25 pages to more

than 300 over several drafts, CCG quarterly reporting requirements that don't match project realities when contracts take years to register, leaving organizations uncertain about what to submit, to whom, and how it will be reviewed. Carnegie Hall and the cultural community look forward to working with DCLA and the City Council to address these issues. These challenges our community faces are not insurmountable, and through cooperation and proper planning, we can solve these problems. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I just wanted to invite Patrick Willingham from the Public Theater to join this panel as well. We squeezed in an extra chair. And feel free to continue.

I want to say hello to Chair Restler, Chair Abreu, Deputy Speaker Dr. Williams, and to the members of the community. My name is David Lowey-Harris. I am the Director of Capital Projects at BAM, and relatively new to the position, all things considered. I want to thank you all personally for how clearly you have paid attention to what is going on, how you have informed yourselves about this, and how your questions reflect

a real insight into what the issues are. For more than 160 years, BAM has served as a cultural anchor in Brooklyn, presenting theater and dance and music and film, while operating a campus of historic theaters and cinemas. Like many other nonprofit cultural institutions in New York City, we're responsible not only for our artistic programming but for the stewardship of these city-owned facilities that must be continuously maintained, modernized, and made accessible to the public. Performing arts institutions in particular operate very complex year-round facilities that require these sustained investments, and unlike commercial presenters, the nonprofit performing arts institutions balance earned revenue with a public service mandate. Beyond presenting a season of performances, we serve as rehearsal hubs, education sites, gathering spaces, and economic drivers for the surrounding small businesses. And without reliable public investment, that broad portfolio of services becomes increasingly difficult to sustain. For cultural institution group members like BAM, the city's capital process plays a regular and essential role in maintaining these spaces, and we are grateful and appreciative for the

support of our city partners. At the same time, we have heard all day about just how difficult it becomes to attain, mobilize, and use the funds to the best benefit of our facilities. The project timelines are incredibly long and just by virtue of their length causing the cost escalation, the contracting delays, and it makes it difficult to even plan these specific projects responsibly and deliver timely upgrades to our facilities. As an immediate example of what we face, you have talked about the ability to use the pass-through process more effectively. There needs to be a consistency in the pass-through process that would allow us to have regular and meaningful planning around how these projects lay out.
Very helpful. Thank you very much.

Good afternoon, Chairs. My name is Jeremy Kaplan. I'm the CEO of Encore Community Services, one of the city's largest contracted nonprofit providers for services for older adults. Among many programs at Encore, our home-delivered meals and congregate meal programs serve about 800,000 meals to older adults annually. I'm here to advocate for Intro 280, put forward by

Council Member Linda Lee, a bill that if passed would have a direct effect on the infrastructural health of many nonprofit organizations. It's a $30 million investment to stabilize home-delivered meal program, a system that is currently being kept afloat by a combination of nonprofit debt and private equity. We must address a fundamental inequity in how our city values nonprofits feeding its elders. For weekday meals, the city reimburses providers at $14.78. However, on the weekends, City Meals on Wheels, whose current capacity only allows for a $10 reimbursement. That difference alone causes a funding deficit for Encore of $550,000 annually. This creates a fundraising trap for us because while we deeply value the role that City Meals plays in our city, their high-profile brand dominates the philanthropic space for senior nutrition. If passed, Intro 280 would do the following: It would help us repair our infrastructural needs. Currently, there is extremely minimal budget for kitchen or truck repairs funded through NYC Aging. At Encore, we waited over three years for a new hotshot van that was awarded to us by the City Council and contracted through DDC. It took three years to get the contract registered and to

get– and to get the van on the street delivering meals. The city expects nonprofits to deliver millions of meals a year without providing the funds to fix the ovens or cook them. Intro 280 would afford our organizations the resources to make much-needed infrastructure and repairs without ever even having to go through the protracted DDC process. We urge you to consider Intro 280. It would be a huge, huge support to older New Yorkers throughout the city.
Thank you so much. Mr. Willingham?

Good afternoon, Chairs and Deputy Speaker. Clearly, I was so excited to attend this hearing that I completely forgot to sign in, so thank you for letting me speak. Thanks for the opportunity to testify today. I am Patrick Willingham, Executive Director of the New York Shakespeare Festival, doing business as the Public Theater. At the outset, I want to acknowledge something fundamental and worth celebrating. New York City has created a program through its nonprofit organizations, particularly members of the Cultural Institutions Group, are entrusted to steward city-owned property and receive capital funding to

maintain public buildings, preserve civic access, and connect New Yorkers to their history and the extraordinary breadth of cultural offerings across the five boroughs. As Executive Director of the Public Theater, I was honored to lead the $85 million renovation of the Delacorte Theater, supported by more than $42 million in city funds and an amount— an equal amount in private philanthropy. It was a self-managed pass-through project with reimbursement through DDC. This partnership is one of New York City's great strengths, but despite many dedicated public servants working hard to help organizations navigate the process, the bureaucracy and inefficiency of the current capital system are hampering the ability of both government and nonprofit partners to deliver projects effectively. Oh, good. I can keep going.
Please.
I thought our time had stopped. because of delays—
[interposing] Council Member Brewer and I were just having a good time. I apologize.

Alright, good to hear. Because of delays and built-in inefficiencies, the public paid more than $2.5 million in interest on loans used to front the city-funded portion of the Delacorte project. We have successfully requisitioned much of our funding, but more than $5 million remains outstanding almost a year after construction completion. Those private dollars spent on interest could have supported additional capital needs or free public programming. It's based on this experience that I'm asking the City Council to partner with capital funding recipients to convene the relevant parties, including DCLA, DDC, MOCS, and OMB, to identify unnecessary bureaucracy such as months-long RFAS reviews, one-at-a-time submission rules, duplicative handoffs, outdated templates, and repeated non-substantive edits. Thanks for your time and consideration.

Yeah, no questions, but, we will continue to have more conversation. And I was excited that the Commissioner himself suggested a roundtable, so I do look forward to convening that roundtable with DDC and the respective agencies that you also listed. So thank you so much as always for

your insight and expertise in helping us think through these problems to find solutions. And I will be at the BAM Gala, so please tell my friends there that I'm going to be late, because I know it has practically started in 15 minutes, but I'm here.

And just want to thank this panel. We really appreciate your insights and I'm excited to visit the Delacorte. I haven't been since the renovation. So hopefully we'll be there soon. But thank you all for your great work and your commitment and contributions to our cultural community. It makes an enormous difference. So thank you for being here today. We have one final person testifying. That is Raul Rivera, who requires no introduction. Something like that. And I would like to acknowledge that Council Member Brewer is back with us. We missed her, but we're happy to have her to close out this hearing. Raul, you have two minutes. Enjoy.

Good afternoon, members of the committee. I am here today in response to the concerns raised in the letter from Council Member Sean Abreu regarding the rideshare platform Empower and its continued operation outside the rules

established by the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission. Council Member Wong, we are asking for your leadership on two urgent matters. First, we urge you to engage directly with Apple Inc. and Google LLC to review Empower's availability on their app store. If a company is operating outside New York City's regulatory framework, it should not be allowed to continue distributing its service unchecked. Removing access through these platforms would protect TLC drivers who are following the law and yet losing thousands of trips and income. Second, we ask you to introduce legislation to protect culturally significant street signage across our city. As reported by CBS News in the headlines, removal of Avenue of Puerto Rico street sign in Brooklyn sparked outrage. The 2023 situation in Bushwick made clear how deeply these signs matter. The community rallied around the preservation of Graham Avenue, known to many as the Avenue of Puerto Rico, because these signage represent heritage, identity, and decades of history for Puerto Rican New Yorkers. We ask you to ensure that what happened then cannot happen again, that cultural designations are respected, preserved, and protected throughout– through clear law. I am

requesting a meeting with your office to discuss further details. Finally, today Mayor Zohran Mamdani laid a wreath at the 9/11 Memorial and his friends with Hasan Piker who said America deserved 9/11. Thank you so much.

Thank you very much. We're now going to transition to people on Zoom. This panel includes– for virtual— so once your name is called, members of staff will unmute you and the Sergeant-of-Arms will set the timer and give you the go-ahead. Please wait for the sergeant to announce you may begin before delivering your testimony. First up, my dear friend Chinita Pointer.
You may begin.
Let me— okay.
We can hear you.
Good afternoon.
Hi, China.
Yes.
Go ahead.

I am. Good afternoon, Chair Restler, Chair Abreu, and Chair Williams, and members of the committees. My name is Chinita Pointer, and I am the CEO and President of the Noel

Pointer Foundation. For over 30 years, we've provided affordable, high-quality string music education to more than 39,000 young people across New York City, primarily serving students from historically underserved communities. Since 2019, our organization has received approximately $13 million in city capital funding to transform the long-vacant DeGraw Firehouse in Cobble Hill into a state-of-the-art music education center. This project is in partnership with the Department of Cultural Affairs and the Department of Design and Construction. Seven years into our project, we have yet to break ground. During that time, construction costs have risen significantly from roughly $11 million to more than $18 million. Unfortunately, we have entered a seemingly never-ending cycle of delays where each delay comes— causes costs to increase, which then requires us to request more funding from the city. Every year of delay means fewer students served and fewer opportunities for the families and young people who rely on us. We thank the Council for bringing attention to the issue of cost escalation and capital project delays. We strongly support Intro 263 and Reso 264. Intro 263 takes an important step toward

fixing delays by requiring a clear strategy to reduce–
[interposing] Thank you. Your time expired.
capital project [inaudible]. Oh, I'm sorry. Okay, well, I want to thank you for your time and consideration.

And we're going to do our best to get that firehouse fully funded and so that we can— that project fully funded so that we can break ground as soon as possible because it's too important, and you have my full commitment. So thank you for being with us.
Thank you.
Next up, we'll go with Adam Ganser from New Yorkers for Parks.
You may begin.

Hey there. Thanks again. I really, really appreciate this hearing, both informative and motivating. My name is Adam Ganser. I'm the Executive Director of New Yorkers for Parks. I think you all know who we are. I'm testifying today in support of the bills and the resos, but also for the capital reforms that are required, not just

across the city but at the Parks Department, I want to bring up a few different things. For the Parks Department, which is notoriously not great at delivering capital projects, the most pressing issue right now is a lack of staffing. Since 2023, the capital division at the Parks Department has lost 60 staffing lines, making it all but impossible for the agency to advance the hundreds of millions of dollars of significant agency infrastructure projects. Second thing I want to mention, this was brought up for the DDC capital project tracker. The Parks Department– the Parks Department also has a capital projects tracker that was meant to provide public information on the status of every capital project and to find out where the delays were. Unfortunately, it's doing neither. It doesn't provide information in a timely manner, and it does nothing to really highlight where the delays are happening, where delays are happening because of other agencies, or whether delays are happening because of scoping changes. I'll mention project delivery methods. DDC and EDC have used design-build, and they've used it successfully. The Parks Department is not doing that. I do not know why, but that should change. And then the last thing

I'll mention is the Capital Projects Task Force. We've heard a lot about it. There was a lot of great work done at the beginning, but then it went dormant. My suggestion is to get all of the public and private sector entities that participated in that, take a look at the recommendations that were made and how they are working or not working, and advance new recommendations.
Thank you. Your time expired.
[inaudible] CDC and authority. Thank you.
Thank you so much, Mr. Ganser, for your thoughtful advocacy for parks. We really appreciate it. Next up, Miss Sophia Harrison.
You may begin.

Hello, Chairs, Deputy Speaker, and Council members. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on the Department of Cultural Affairs capital funding process. My name is Sophia Harrison. I am the Executive Director of Arts House Schools of Music, Dance, and Fine Arts in Coney Island, Brooklyn, serving the 47th Council District.

In 2005, Arts House Schools relocated and entered into a 10-year lease that with two five-year options, creating potential for a 20-year tenancy. We structured this lease intentionally, understanding that we would be seeking public capital funds and that the useful life of most capital projects is approximately 20 years. With support from our council member and borough president, we began the DCLA capital process for projects estimated between $500,000 to $750,000. What we did not realize was that construction would take up to five years to begin and that the project's useful life would not start until construction was complete. We were told that because we must remain operational during construction, the timeline could be even longer, effectively requiring a 30 to 35-year lease commitment. For a nonprofit tenant in a privately owned space, this is simply unrealistic. My landlord ultimately chose not to move forward due to DCLA's lease restrictions, including requirements for how the space could be used after our lease ends. As a result, despite elected funding support, our organization could not access city capital dollars. Under the current DCLA capital process, timelines and

restrictions make participation impractical, if not impossible, for nonprofit cultural organizations that lease privately owned space. In effect, the system primarily benefits organizations located on city-owned property or those that own their own buildings. This creates a significant barrier for community-based cultural institutions like ours which serve neighborhoods with limited access to the arts, but lack the resources to open property. Compounding this challenge, DCLA no longer supports building acquisition, removing a pathway that once helped organizations establish long-term stability.
Thank you. Your time expired.
I urge the council to modernize this process so that leased nonprofit spaces can realistically participate in the city capital funding. Thank you.
Thank you so much, Ms. Harrison. We really appreciate your testimony. It's a very important point that you raise. And next up, Jason Pastore from—
[interposing] You may begin—
Environmental Contractors Association.

Good afternoon, everybody, Chairs Restler, Abreu, and Williams, and members of the committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Jason Pastore, and I'm testifying on behalf of the Environmental Contractors Association, also known as the ECA. We're the Association for Unionized Contractors who perform environmental hazard remediation, including asbestos, mold, and lead. The core priority of the ECA is a safe, efficient, and timely removal of asbestos at construction sites. Asbestos abatement is a prerequisite for most construction activity, making this work critical to the timely start of projects. As you can imagine, it is unsafe for construction to move forward while asbestos remains in place. Therefore, it must be removed prior to other work. New York City maintains strict regulations for the removal of asbestos-containing materials through the Asbestos Control Program, overseen by the Department of Environmental Protection. However, due to severe staffing shortages at the DEP, approval timelines have increased dramatically. What was once a few-week

process can now take many months. These delays significantly impact the capital projects at schools, NYCHA housing, hospitals, and other critical infrastructure, because no construction can occur until DEP issues asbestos removal permits. These delays are incredibly financially costly for the agencies we work with. Prolonged approval times also increase potential exposure risks for workers and the public, raising serious public health concerns. Not only do these delays make construction more expensive for the city, but they also put city workers and residents at risk of exposure to asbestos. Furthermore, the length of review process rarely— is rarely due to safety concerns with plans. In fact, most delays are due to technicalities and not deviations from regulations. We are rarely asking to perform work that has not already been specifically regulated by the DEP. To address this issue, the ECA has been working with Council Member De La Rosa and the City Council Legislative Division to develop legislation that would allow for the use of professional certification, also known as ProCert or self-certification for asbestos approvals. Professional certification is already used in areas

across the city. It would allow contractors to remove asbestos without having to wait many months for DEP approvals. Importantly, this approach maintains strong safety safeguards. All asbestos abatement work would include audits of forms, maintain third-party air monitoring, and ensure DEP retains—
Thank you, your time expired.
Thank you.

Thank you so much for that great testimony. Incredibly helpful. Next up, our final person from the day is Fabian Derewiecki. I think I butchered that, and I apologize, Fabian, from Local 785. I'm blaming Johari's [sp?] handwriting here.
You may begin.

No worries, it's Fabian Derewiecki and it's Local 78, and thank you for the opportunity to speak today about the construction and contracting delays. My name is Fabian Derewiecki. I'm here on behalf of Local 78, Asbestos, Lead, and Hazardous Waste Laborers Union. Our members are on the ground performing hazardous material remediation work, handling asbestos, lead,

and mold removal across construction sites throughout New York City. For us, one issue consistently stands out. Asbestos abatement is often the first step in any construction project, and what the— that step is delayed— when that step is delayed, everything else is pushed back with it. The city has a strong regulatory framework in place through the Department of Environmental Protection Asbestos Control Program, but in practice, the process has slowed significantly. Due to the staffing shortages at DEP, approvals that once took a matter of weeks now are now stretching into months. These delays stall projects at public schools, public housing developments, hospitals, and other essential facilities because no construction activity can begin without the required permits. The result is higher costs and prolonged timelines across the board. From our perspective, these delays also carry real safety implications. The longer asbestos remains in place, the longer workers are— and nearby residents face potential exposure. That is a serious public health concern, particularly in communities like NYCHA developments where residents are already vulnerable. It is important to note that these holdups are rarely

about unsafe and inadequate plans. In most cases, contractors are submitting work plans that already comply with DEP-established rules. The delays tend to come from administrative bottlenecks and technical reviews issues, not from safety problems. To help address this, Local 78 has been working with Council Member De La Rosa and Council Legislative Division on the proposal to allow for professional certification, also called ProCert, in the asbestos permitting process. This approach would enable qualified professionals to certify their own plans and move forward without waiting months for formal approvals. We believe that this practical solution would help keep projects on track, reduce unnecessary costs, and better protect—
Thank you, your time expired.
Thank you.

We greatly appreciate the testimony from Local 78. It is really helpful as we move forward with trying to improve the capital project delivery system and in our conversations with DDC. I'd like to turn it over to Council Member Brewer for a comment.

Thank you very much. I just— in terms of the woman who has a rental in a building. It's an ongoing problem because the city will take your walls first, and so they do not want somebody else to spend the money. What we've been able to do in some cases, if the building has a space that is just for you, you can become a co-op. We've been able to do it in certain churches and synagogues on the ground floor where that institution is their own nonprofit. You have to do a second nonprofit, and then you can spend the city capital money. Just something to think about for the future. Thank you.

And I'll just add for a moment, you know, it was a— one of the many, many, many poor decisions from the previous administration was to prohibit cultural institutions from purchasing– from acquiring property that they could own. We want every nonprofit in New York City to have access to own property, and be able to stably and affordably remain in our communities. One of the ways that we've gotten around that in District 33 is that nonprofit organizations have purchased the property via a loan, and then we've given money to

reimburse the purchase, essentially covering the loan or the mortgage, which OMB has permitted, just not— it's not directly going to the acquisition itself. So if— and if and until when DCLA changes their policy, which I hope will happen in the very near future, that is an end around that we had identified for Ms. Harrison in case that is helpful. With that, we're gonna adjourn this hearing. I want to thank my co-chairs, Majority Leader Abreu, Deputy Speaker Williams, Council Member Brewer. Always great to have you. And thank you to the staff who did a great job in preparing. Hope you all have a wonderful day. And thank you to the Sergeant-of-Arms for a complicated hearing. You guys did a great job. Thank you. [gavel]

I'm keeping it moving in case anybody was wondering. We're ready? Let's go.

that New Yorkers know that, A, there's no wrong door, and B, that they can turn to an agency they trust to get the help they need. I just want to be sure it's written in a way that doesn't slow down that relief, that speeds it up instead.

No, I appreciate that, and nothing stops us. Let me share a little bit more on how I see the sort of differences, because you're absolutely right. Just about everything we do, if not everything we do, the state has authority to do as well. Deceptive practices, AG can take it on. Unconscionable practices, AG can take it on, etc., etc. I think the difference here is that our expectation, which could be wrong, is that the vast majority of complaints we get are going to be about rate increases and claim denials. And with respect to rate increases, those are not just— it's not just sort of a general deceptive practice. Those are

specifically regulated and either authorized or not authorized by the state. That is just an area– we can't— my understanding is we couldn't allege that a rate increase is deceptive, for example, or unconscionable if the state specifically authorized a rate increase. Now, that might be different if an insurance says— if insurer says, get your first month of auto insurance free. That's very much in our— and they don't give it free. Very much in our wheelhouse. We have the authority. We would talk to the state because, you know, there's overlapping jurisdiction, but that's well within our wheelhouse.
